title: Solve Inequalities Using Technology
overview: Equations ask *where* a polynomial equals zero; **inequalities** ask *where it is positive or negative*. In this section you will learn to describe solutions using intervals, see how the zeros split the $x$-axis into regions of constant sign, and use graphs and technology to solve polynomial inequalities — including real models of revenue and amusement-park rides.
objectives: Explain the difference between a polynomial equation and a polynomial inequality.
Write solutions using inequality, interval and set notation and on a number line.
Explain how the real zeros divide the $x$-axis into intervals of constant sign.
Solve polynomial inequalities graphically, by hand and with technology.
Solve inequalities of the form $P(x) \ge Q(x)$ by rearranging or comparing graphs.
Solve problems involving polynomial inequalities and interpret the answers.

lessons.title: Polynomial inequalities and how to write their solutions
lessons.body:
A **polynomial inequality** is what you get when the equal sign of a polynomial equation is replaced by $<$, $\le$, $>$ or $\ge$. For example, $x^3 - 4x > 0$.

An equation usually has a few solutions; an inequality usually has **intervals** of solutions. There are three common ways to write them:

| Words | Inequality | Interval notation | Number line |
|---|---|---|---|
| between $-2$ and $3$, not including the ends | $-2 < x < 3$ | $(-2, 3)$ | open dots at $-2$ and $3$, shaded between |
| $-2$ up to $3$, including both | $-2 \le x \le 3$ | $[-2, 3]$ | closed dots, shaded between |
| greater than $5$ | $x > 5$ | $(5, \infty)$ | open dot at $5$, arrow right |
| at most $-1$ | $x \le -1$ | $(-\infty, -1]$ | closed dot at $-1$, arrow left |
| two separate pieces | $x < -2$ or $x > 3$ | $(-\infty, -2) \cup (3, \infty)$ | two shaded rays |

* Round brackets / open dots: the endpoint is **not** included ($<$, $>$). Infinity always takes a round bracket.
* Square brackets / closed dots: the endpoint **is** included ($\le$, $\ge$).
* $\cup$ means "or" (union of intervals).

**Set notation** describes the same thing: $\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid x < -2 \text{ or } x > 3\}$.

lessons.title: The zeros split the x-axis into intervals
lessons.body:
A polynomial graph is a smooth unbroken curve. It can only change from positive to negative (or back) by passing through the $x$-axis — that is, at a **zero**. So:

> Between two consecutive zeros, a polynomial has **one sign** throughout.

For $P(x) = (x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)$ the zeros $-1$, $2$, $3$ split the axis into four intervals:

| Interval | $(-\infty, -1)$ | $(-1, 2)$ | $(2, 3)$ | $(3, \infty)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Test value | $-2$ | $0$ | $2.5$ | $4$ |
| Sign of $P(x)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |
| Graph is | below axis | above | below | above |

```plot
title: y = (x + 1)(x − 2)(x − 3): positive where the graph is above the x-axis
f: (x+1)*(x-2)*(x-3)
domain: -2, 4.5
range: -12, 10
ticks: 1, 2
points: (-1,0), (2,0), (3,0)
```

So $(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 3) > 0$ for $-1 < x < 2$ or $x > 3$, i.e. $(-1, 2) \cup (3, \infty)$.

lessons.title: Solving an inequality graphically
lessons.body:
**Steps**

1. Rearrange so one side is $0$: e.g. $P(x) \ge 0$. (Or keep both sides and compare two graphs — see below.)
2. Graph $y = P(x)$ (by hand from its factors, or with technology).
3. Find the zeros (exactly if it factors; otherwise with the **zero** operation, rounded as asked).
4. Read the intervals where the graph is **above** the axis ($> 0$) or **below** it ($< 0$).
5. Include the zeros if the inequality is $\le$ or $\ge$.

**Two-graph method:** to solve $P(x) \ge k$ or $P(x) \ge Q(x)$, graph both sides and find where one graph is above the other. The boundary points are the **intersection points**.

**Example:** solve $x^2 + 3x - 5 > 0$. The zeros (technology, or the quadratic formula) are $x \approx -4.2$ and $x \approx 1.2$. The parabola opens up, so it is above the axis outside the zeros:

$$x < -4.2 \text{ or } x > 1.2$$

lessons.title: Using technology effectively
lessons.body:
Most polynomial inequalities that come from real data don't factor, so you need technology.

**Graphing calculator / graphing software**
* Enter $y = P(x)$, choose a window that shows every $x$-intercept and the turning points.
* Use **zero** (or *root*) to find each $x$-intercept; round as instructed.
* Read off the intervals.

**Computer algebra system (CAS)** or a **table of values**
* Solve $P(x) = 0$ numerically to get the boundary points.
* Test one value in each interval: if the inequality is true there, the whole interval is a solution.

**Example:** solve $x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 2 \ge 0$.

```plot
f: x^3 - 2*x^2 - 5*x + 2
domain: -2.5, 4
range: -12, 8
points: (-1.681,0), (0.358,0), (3.323,0)
```

Zeros $\approx -1.7,\ 0.4,\ 3.3$. The graph is above (or on) the axis on $[-1.7, 0.4]$ and $[3.3, \infty)$.

lessons.title: Applications: when is a model above a target?
lessons.body:
Inequalities answer questions like "**when** will sales be at least \$100 million?" or "**for how long** is a ride higher than 15 m?"

**Example:** the yearly revenue of an MP3 player company is $R(t) = t^3 - 0.8t^2 + 2t - 1$ million dollars, $t$ years after 2003. When is $R(t) \ge 100$?

* Rearrange: $t^3 - 0.8t^2 + 2t - 101 \ge 0$.
* Graph and find the zero: $t \approx 4.8$.
* The graph is above the axis for $t > 4.8$.

So revenue is at least \$100 million from about $4.8$ years after 2003 — late in 2007 — onward (as long as the model stays valid).

> In context, also state the **domain** that makes sense (e.g. $t \ge 0$) and question whether the model stays realistic far into the future.

keyTerms.definition: An inequality containing a polynomial, such as $x^3 - 4x \ge 0$.
Writing a set of real numbers using brackets, e.g. $(-2, 3]$; round brackets exclude endpoints, square brackets include them.
A number chosen inside an interval to determine the sign of the polynomial there.

formulas.name: Sign rule
formulas.latex: \text{between consecutive zeros, } P(x) \text{ keeps one sign}
formulas.meaning: So test one value per interval.

formulas.name: Rearranging
formulas.meaning: Graph the difference, or graph both and compare.

workedExamples.title: Reading the solution from a factored graph
steps: Zeros: $-1$, $2$, $3$. Leading coefficient positive, degree 3: the graph starts below the axis on the left and ends above on the right.

workedExamples.title: A quartic with technology
steps: Graph $y = 2x^4 + 5x^3 - 3x^2 - 15x - 9$. The zeros are approximately $-1.7$, $-1.5$, $-1$ and $1.7$. (In fact it factors as $(2x + 3)(x + 1)(x^2 - 3)$, so the zeros are exactly $\pm\sqrt3$, $-\tfrac32$ and $-1$.)
Positive leading coefficient, even degree: up on both ends. Signs: $+, -, +, -, +$ across the five intervals.

workedExamples.title: Comparing two sides
workedExamples.problem: Solve $x^3 + 3x \le 8x^2 - 9$. Round to one decimal place.
steps: Cubic with positive leading coefficient: below the axis on $(-\infty, -0.9)$ and $(1.4, 7.4)$.

workedExamples.title: A water ride
workedExamples.problem: The height of a water-tube ride is $h(t) = -0.002t^4 + 0.104t^3 - 1.69t^2 + 8.5t + 9$ metres after $t$ seconds, $0 \le t \le 25$. When are riders more than $15$ m above the ground?
steps: The graph of $h$ is above $y = 15$ between the first two and between the last two.

misconceptions.fact: A product is positive when both factors have the **same** sign: $x < 1$ or $x > 4$. Check with a graph or test values.

misconceptions.myth: For $\le$, use round brackets at the zeros.
misconceptions.fact: $\le$ and $\ge$ **include** the zeros: use square brackets and closed dots.
Infinity is not a number you can reach; always use a round bracket: $[3, \infty)$.

misconceptions.myth: To solve $P(x) > 5$, find the zeros of $P(x)$.
misconceptions.fact: Find where $P(x) = 5$, i.e. the zeros of $P(x) - 5$ (or the intersections with $y = 5$).
At a zero of **even** order the sign does **not** change (the graph touches and turns back). Test every interval.

realWorld.title: Business targets
realWorld.body: Companies solve inequalities to find when revenue exceeds a target or when costs stay below a budget.

realWorld.title: Amusement park safety
realWorld.body: Ride designers check when riders are above certain heights or below certain speeds — inequalities on polynomial models.

realWorld.title: Engineering tolerances
realWorld.body: A part is acceptable if a measurement stays within a range; that is an inequality on a model of the measurement.

realWorld.title: Medicine
realWorld.body: A drug is effective while its concentration stays above a threshold; solving the inequality gives the effective time window.

practice.question: Write in interval notation: $-3 < x \le 2$ or $x > 5$.
The zeros of a cubic with positive leading coefficient are $-7$, $0$ and $2$. List the intervals and the sign of the function on each.
practice.hint: Start from the left end behaviour.

practice.question: Solve $(x + 2)(x - 1)(x - 4) < 0$.
practice.hint: Use the sign pattern for a positive cubic.

practice.question: Solve $x^3 - 6x + 2 \ge 0$ using technology. Round to one decimal place.
Solve $x^3 - 2x^2 - 3x + 1 < 0$. Round to one decimal place.
Explain why the solution of $(x - 3)^2(x + 1) \ge 0$ is $x \ge -1$.
practice.solution: $(x - 3)^2 \ge 0$ for all $x$, so the sign is controlled by $x + 1$: the product is $\ge 0$ exactly when $x + 1 \ge 0$ (and at $x = 3$, where it equals $0$, which is already included). So $x \ge -1$.

summary: A polynomial inequality's solution is usually a union of intervals; write it with inequalities, interval notation, set notation or a number line.
The real zeros split the $x$-axis into intervals on which the polynomial keeps one sign.
Graphically: $P(x) > 0$ where the graph is above the $x$-axis, $P(x) < 0$ where it is below. Include zeros for $\le$ and $\ge$.
Use technology to find zeros that are not exact; round as asked.
For $P(x) \ge Q(x)$, solve $P(x) - Q(x) \ge 0$ or compare the two graphs.

questions.text: The $x$-intercepts of the graph of a cubic function $y = f(x)$ with a **positive** leading coefficient are $-{{a}}$, ${{b}}$ and ${{c}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write the intervals into which the $x$-axis is divided.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the sign of $f(x)$ on each interval and explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The intercepts divide the $x$-axis into four intervals:
$(-\infty, -{{a}})$, $(-{{a}}, {{b}})$, $({{b}}, {{c}})$, $({{c}}, \infty)$.

(b) A cubic with positive leading coefficient goes from below the axis (left) to above (right), changing sign at each simple zero:

| Interval | $(-\infty, -{{a}})$ | $(-{{a}}, {{b}})$ | $({{b}}, {{c}})$ | $({{c}}, \infty)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sign of $f(x)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

(c) $f(x) > 0$ for $-{{a}} < x < {{b}}$ or $x > {{c}}$: $(-{{a}}, {{b}}) \cup ({{c}}, \infty)$.

rubric.point: Correct signs, with reasoning from end behaviour
Correct solution of $f(x) > 0$ in interval notation

questions.text: A solution is described in words as: \"all real numbers greater than $-{{a}}$ and less than or equal to ${{b}}$, or greater than or equal to ${{c}}$.\"

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe how it would look on a number line, explaining each endpoint.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $-{{a}} < x \le {{b}}$ or $x \ge {{c}}$

(b) $(-{{a}}, {{b}}] \cup [{{c}}, \infty)$

(c) $\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid -{{a}} < x \le {{b}} \text{ or } x \ge {{c}}\}$

(d) Open dot at $-{{a}}$, closed dot at ${{b}}$, shading between them; closed dot at ${{c}}$ with shading (an arrow) to the right.

Round bracket/open dot at $-{{a}}$ because it is not included ("greater than"); square brackets/closed dots at ${{b}}$ and ${{c}}$ because they are included; round bracket at $\infty$ because infinity is never reached.

rubric.point: Correct number line description with explanation of open/closed dots

questions.text:
The graph of $y = P(x)$, a cubic polynomial, is shown.

```plot
f: (x+{{A}})*(x-{{B}})*(x-{{C}})
domain: -5, 7
points: (-{{A}},0), ({{B}},0), ({{C}},0)
```
questions.modelAnswer:
The zeros are $-{{A}}$, ${{B}}$ and ${{C}}$.

The graph rises to the right (positive leading coefficient), so it is below the axis on the far left, then above, below, above:

| Interval | $(-\infty, -{{A}})$ | $(-{{A}}, {{B}})$ | $({{B}}, {{C}})$ | $({{C}}, \infty)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Graph | below | above | below | above |

(a) $P(x) \ge 0$ (on or above the axis, zeros included): $-{{A}} \le x \le {{B}}$ or $x \ge {{C}}$, i.e. $[-{{A}}, {{B}}] \cup [{{C}}, \infty)$.

(b) $P(x) < 0$ (strictly below, zeros excluded): $x < -{{A}}$ or ${{B}} < x < {{C}}$, i.e. $(-\infty, -{{A}}) \cup ({{B}}, {{C}})$.

rubric.point: Reads the zeros from the graph

questions.text: Solve $x^2 + 3x - 5 > 0$. Round the zeros to one decimal place, and explain how the graph shows your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
Zeros of $x^2 + 3x - 5$: $x = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 20}}{2} = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{29}}{2}$, so $x \approx -4.2$ and $x \approx 1.2$ (or use the zero operation).

The parabola opens upward, so it is **above** the $x$-axis to the left of the smaller zero and to the right of the larger zero.

$$x < -4.2 \text{ or } x > 1.2$$

rubric.point: Finds both zeros to one decimal place
Uses the shape of the graph to choose intervals

questions.modelAnswer:
Graph $y = 2x^3 - 13x^2 + 17x + 12$ and find the zeros: $x = -0.5$, $3$ and $4$. (Check: it factors as $(2x + 1)(x - 3)(x - 4)$.)

Positive leading coefficient, cubic: below the axis on the far left, then above, below, above.

| Interval | $(-\infty, -0.5)$ | $(-0.5, 3)$ | $(3, 4)$ | $(4, \infty)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sign | $-$ | $+$ | $-$ | $+$ |

Include the zeros ($\le$): $x \le -0.5$ or $3 \le x \le 4$, i.e. $(-\infty, -0.5] \cup [3, 4]$.

rubric.point: Determines the sign on each interval

questions.text: Use technology to solve $x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 2 \ge 0$. Round to one decimal place.
questions.modelAnswer:
Graph $y = x^3 - 2x^2 - 5x + 2$ and use the zero operation: $x \approx -1.7$, $0.4$, $3.3$.

The graph is on or above the $x$-axis between the first two zeros and to the right of the third.

$$-1.7 \le x \le 0.4 \text{ or } x \ge 3.3$$

rubric.point: Finds all three zeros to one decimal place
Identifies where the graph is above the axis

questions.modelAnswer:
Graphing (or testing rational zeros) gives zeros $-4$, $-\tfrac13$ and $3$; indeed $3x^3 + 4x^2 - 35x - 12 = (x + 4)(3x + 1)(x - 3)$.

Positive cubic: signs $-, +, -, +$ on $(-\infty, -4)$, $(-4, -\tfrac13)$, $(-\tfrac13, 3)$, $(3, \infty)$.

$$-4 < x < -\tfrac13 \text{ or } x > 3$$

parts.label: a
parts.text: Give the right-hand endpoint of the solution to one decimal place.

questions.modelAnswer:
Graphing shows zeros at about $-2.2$, $-1$ and $2.2$, with the graph **touching** the axis at $x = -1$.

It factors: $-x^4 - 2x^3 + 4x^2 + 10x + 5 = -(x + 1)^2(x^2 - 5)$.

So $-(x + 1)^2(x^2 - 5) \ge 0 \iff (x + 1)^2(x^2 - 5) \le 0$. Since $(x + 1)^2 \ge 0$, this holds when $x^2 - 5 \le 0$ or $x = -1$:

$$-\sqrt5 \le x \le \sqrt5 \quad (\approx -2.2 \le x \le 2.2)$$

At $x = -1$ (a zero of order 2) the graph touches the axis but does **not** change sign — the function is $\ge 0$ on both sides, so the solution is one unbroken interval.

rubric.point: Explains why the sign does not change at $x = -1$

questions.text: Solve $x^3 + 3x \le 8x^2 - 9$. Round answers to one decimal place.
questions.modelAnswer:
Rearrange: $x^3 - 8x^2 + 3x + 9 \le 0$.

Graph $y = x^3 - 8x^2 + 3x + 9$; zeros $\approx -0.9$, $1.4$, $7.4$.

Positive cubic: below the axis on $(-\infty, -0.9)$ and $(1.4, 7.4)$.

$$x \le -0.9 \text{ or } 1.4 \le x \le 7.4$$

(Alternatively graph $y = x^3 + 3x$ and $y = 8x^2 - 9$ and find where the first is on or below the second.)

rubric.point: Rearranges to compare with zero (or uses two graphs)

questions.text: Solve $-x^4 + 3x^3 + 9x^2 > 5x + 5$. Round to one decimal place.
questions.modelAnswer:
Rearrange: $-x^4 + 3x^3 + 9x^2 - 5x - 5 > 0$.

Graph $y = -x^4 + 3x^3 + 9x^2 - 5x - 5$; zeros $\approx -2.0$, $-0.6$, $0.9$, $4.7$.

Negative leading coefficient, even degree: down on both ends, so the signs across the five intervals are $-, +, -, +, -$.

$$-2.0 < x < -0.6 \text{ or } 0.9 < x < 4.7$$

rubric.point: Uses end behaviour / test values to get the signs

questions.text: An electronics manufacturer models yearly revenue from MP3 players by $R(t) = t^3 - 0.8t^2 + 2t - 1$, in millions of dollars, where $t$ is the number of years since 2003.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write an inequality for when yearly revenue is \$100 million or more.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Solve it and interpret the answer. Give the boundary value of $t$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Is the model likely to remain valid for 20 years? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) $t^3 - 0.8t^2 + 2t - 1 \ge 100$

(b) Rearrange: $t^3 - 0.8t^2 + 2t - 101 \ge 0$. Graph $y = t^3 - 0.8t^2 + 2t - 101$; its only real zero is $t \approx 4.8$. The graph is above the axis to the right of this zero, so $t \ge 4.8$.

Revenue is at least \$100 million from about $4.8$ years after 2003 (late 2007) onward.

(c) Probably not: the cubic model keeps increasing without limit, but real sales of a product eventually level off or fall (new technology replaces it). The model is only reliable for a limited time.

rubric.point: Reasonable comment on the validity of the model

questions.text: A section of a water-tube ride is modelled by $h(t) = -0.002t^4 + 0.104t^3 - 1.69t^2 + 8.5t + 9$, where $h$ is the height in metres and $t$ is the time in seconds, $0 \le t \le 25$. When will riders be more than $15$ m above the ground?

parts.label: a
parts.text: How long, in total, are riders above 15 m? (Round to one decimal place.)

questions.modelAnswer:
Solve $h(t) > 15$, i.e. $-0.002t^4 + 0.104t^3 - 1.69t^2 + 8.5t - 6 > 0$.

Graph $y = h(t)$ and $y = 15$ for $0 \le t \le 25$ (or graph $y = h(t) - 15$). The intersection points are at $t \approx 0.8$, $7.6$, $20.0$ and $23.6$.

The ride is above $15$ m between the first pair and between the second pair:

$$0.8 < t < 7.6 \quad\text{or}\quad 20.0 < t < 23.6 \text{ (seconds)}$$

rubric.point: Uses technology to find all four boundary times
Answer stated in context with units

questions.text: Explain the difference between a polynomial equation and a polynomial inequality. Support your answer with an example of each, including what their solutions look like.
questions.modelAnswer:
A polynomial **equation** states that a polynomial equals something (usually $0$), e.g. $x^2 - 4 = 0$. Its solution is a finite set of values: $x = \pm2$. These are the $x$-intercepts of $y = x^2 - 4$.

A polynomial **inequality** uses $<$, $\le$, $>$ or $\ge$, e.g. $x^2 - 4 < 0$. Its solution is usually one or more **intervals**: $-2 < x < 2$, the $x$-values where the graph is below the $x$-axis.

The equation's roots are the **boundary points** of the inequality's solution intervals.

rubric.point: Correct description and example of an equation and its solution
Correct description and example of an inequality and its interval solution
Explains the connection (roots are boundary points)

questions.text: Describe the connection between the solution of a polynomial inequality and the graph of the corresponding function. What role do the real roots of the related equation play? Use $f(x) = x(x - 3)(x + 2)$ to illustrate.
questions.modelAnswer:
The solution of $f(x) > 0$ is the set of $x$-values where the graph of $y = f(x)$ is **above** the $x$-axis; $f(x) < 0$ is where it is **below**.

The real roots of $f(x) = 0$ — here $-2$, $0$, $3$ — are the $x$-intercepts. They are the only places the graph can change from above to below, so they split the axis into intervals of constant sign and form the **endpoints** of the solution intervals. Whether the endpoints are included depends on whether the inequality is strict.

For $f(x) = x(x - 3)(x + 2)$ (positive cubic): $f(x) > 0$ on $(-2, 0) \cup (3, \infty)$ and $f(x) \le 0$ on $(-\infty, -2] \cup [0, 3]$.

rubric.point: Explains the roots as boundaries where the sign can change

questions.text: Describe how you would use technology to solve $1.2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3.5x - 2 \ge 0$, then carry out your plan. Round to one decimal place.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Plan:** enter $y = 1.2x^3 + 5x^2 - 3.5x - 2$ in a graphing calculator or graphing software. Choose a window showing all intercepts (e.g. $x \in [-6, 3]$, $y \in [-10, 30]$). Use the zero operation near each $x$-intercept. Then read the intervals where the graph is on or above the axis. (With a CAS: solve the equation numerically, then test a value in each interval.)

**Result:** zeros $\approx -4.7$, $-0.4$, $0.9$. Positive cubic → signs $-, +, -, +$.

$$-4.7 \le x \le -0.4 \text{ or } x \ge 0.9$$

rubric.point: Clear description of the technology steps (graph, window, zero operation)

questions.text: Create an equation for a cubic function $y = f(x)$ such that $f(x) < 0$ when $-4 < x < 3$ or $x > 7$, and $f(x) > 0$ when $x < -4$ or $3 < x < 7$. Explain how your equation produces exactly these intervals, and describe its graph.
questions.modelAnswer:
The sign changes at $-4$, $3$ and $7$, so these are the zeros: factors $(x + 4)$, $(x - 3)$, $(x - 7)$.

For large $x$ the function is negative, and for very negative $x$ it is positive: the end behaviour is "up on the left, down on the right", so the leading coefficient is **negative**.

$$f(x) = -(x + 4)(x - 3)(x - 7)$$ (any $f(x) = k(x + 4)(x - 3)(x - 7)$ with $k < 0$ works).

Check with test values: $f(0) = -(4)(-3)(-7) = -84 < 0$ ✓ (in $(-4, 3)$); $f(5) = -(9)(2)(-2) = 36 > 0$ ✓.

The graph comes down from the upper left, crosses the axis at $-4$, rises to cross again at $3$, then falls back through $7$ and continues downward.

rubric.point: Identifies the zeros from the sign changes
Chooses a negative leading coefficient with a reason
Valid equation verified with test values

questions.text: Solve $x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 7 < 0$ using technology. Round to one decimal place.
questions.modelAnswer:
Graph $y = x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x - 7$; zeros $\approx -3.6$, $-1.1$, $1.7$.

Positive cubic: below the axis on $(-\infty, -3.6)$ and $(-1.1, 1.7)$.

$$x < -3.6 \text{ or } -1.1 < x < 1.7$$

questions.text: Solve $2x^4 + 5x^3 - 3x^2 - 15x - 9 \ge 0$. Use technology to find the zeros, then confirm them by factoring.
questions.modelAnswer:
Graph $y = 2x^4 + 5x^3 - 3x^2 - 15x - 9$: zeros $\approx -1.7$, $-1.5$, $-1$, $1.7$.

**Confirm by factoring:** $P(-1) = 2 - 5 - 3 + 15 - 9 = 0$, so $x + 1$ is a factor. Dividing gives $2x^3 + 3x^2 - 6x - 9 = x^2(2x + 3) - 3(2x + 3) = (2x + 3)(x^2 - 3)$.
So $P(x) = (x + 1)(2x + 3)(x^2 - 3)$, with zeros $-1$, $-\tfrac32$, $\pm\sqrt3 \approx \pm1.7$ ✓

Positive even-degree polynomial: signs $+, -, +, -, +$.

$$x \le -\sqrt3 \;\text{ or }\; -\tfrac32 \le x \le -1 \;\text{ or }\; x \ge \sqrt3$$
(about $x \le -1.7$, $-1.5 \le x \le -1$, $x \ge 1.7$)

rubric.point: Finds the four zeros with technology
